script.opening: (Mother, frightened, lowered voice.) "Doctor, I don’t know what’s happening to my son. Over the last few weeks he’s changed completely — he won’t sleep, he’s stopped going to college, and now he’s saying people are watching him through the television, that it’s sending him messages. He’s put furniture against his door. He won’t talk to me properly. Is he on drugs? Is he having a breakdown? I’m scared and I don’t know who to call."

facts.text: If explored: weeks of progressive change — social withdrawal, insomnia, auditory hallucinations (voices), persecutory delusions (being watched/monitored), ideas of reference (TV sending messages), functional decline (left college), self-protective behaviour (barricading). This is a probable FIRST EPISODE OF PSYCHOSIS — a serious, treatable condition where early intervention matters.

Must be assessed via the mother (and ideally the young person if reachable): any thoughts/acts of self-harm or suicide, any aggression or threat to others, command hallucinations telling him to act, ability to keep safe, insight, and whether he is eating/drinking. Currently no expressed intent or violence, but distress and barricading raise concern.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the mother carries guilt and a specific fear she hasn’t voiced: his father had "a breakdown" (possible family history of psychosis/schizophrenia) and she is terrified Daniel "has the same thing" and "will be locked away forever". She also feels she caused it by "not noticing the cannabis sooner". These fears shape her questions and need addressing.

Heavy cannabis use is relevant (a risk factor/precipitant), but framing this as "just drugs / his fault" would be wrong and stigmatising; psychosis needs assessment regardless. The family history (if elicited) is sensitive.

Officially: to know if it’s drugs or a breakdown and who to call. What is needed: recognition of probable first-episode psychosis, an urgent same-day mental-health assessment (early intervention/crisis pathway), a safety/risk assessment, and compassionate handling of her guilt and the "locked away forever" fear.

ice.ideas: Either he’s on drugs or he’s "having a breakdown"; she doesn’t know who to call.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — guilt that she "caused it" by missing the cannabis, and unspoken terror that he has inherited his father’s "breakdown" (possible family psychosis) and will be "locked away forever".
ice.expectations: To be told what it is and who to call. What is actually needed: recognition of probable first-episode psychosis, urgent mental-health assessment, a risk/safety plan, and her guilt and fears addressed.

cues: Weeks of withdrawal + voices + "watched through the TV" + barricading in a 17-year-old — probable first-episode psychosis; urgent, not routine.
"Is it the drugs? Is it my fault?" — guilt and the inheritance fear (father’s "breakdown") to surface and address.
Heavy cannabis + family history — relevant but must not become a blaming "it’s just drugs" narrative.

checkpoints.text: Recognises probable FIRST-EPISODE PSYCHOSIS from the collateral history (hallucinations, persecutory/referential delusions, functional decline, withdrawal, insomnia over weeks) and treats it as a serious, treatable condition needing urgent specialist assessment — not "just drugs" or "a phase"

Conducts a RISK ASSESSMENT through the mother (and the young person if reachable): self-harm/suicide, harm to others, command hallucinations, ability to stay safe, insight, eating/drinking/sleeping, and the immediate safety of the household

Arranges URGENT same-day mental-health assessment via the appropriate pathway: Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) service / CAMHS / crisis team (NICE CG155: a first presentation of sustained psychotic symptoms is referred urgently to CAMHS or, from age 14, an EIP service; with raised risk the crisis team or on-call CAMHS assesses the same day), recognising EIP’s remit and that early treatment improves outcomes; does NOT start an antipsychotic in primary care (NICE CG155: only in consultation with a consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist); involves the GP/duty doctor and, if immediate danger, emergency services

Handles the cannabis appropriately: notes it as a relevant precipitant/risk factor and part of the picture, without reducing the presentation to "drug-induced/his fault"; psychosis is assessed and treated regardless of cause

Plans engagement of a young person who won’t come to the phone: how assessment can happen (home-based/crisis assessment), the mother’s role, de-escalation/safety at home, and what to do if he deteriorates or there is immediate risk (999/police if danger)

Responds to the mother’s fear and exhaustion with compassion; surfaces and addresses the guilt ("not my fault") and the "locked away forever" fear with honest, hopeful information about treatment and recovery
Avoids stigmatising language; frames psychosis as an illness that is treatable and where early help leads to better outcomes, supporting both mother and son

Safety-nets and coordinates clearly: the urgent assessment route and timeframe, crisis numbers, when to call 999/police (immediate danger to self/others), support for the mother/family, and documented follow-up — a concrete plan, not just information

worked.txt: "Thank you for ringing — this sounds frightening and you’ve done exactly the right thing. From what you’re describing, Daniel may be experiencing something we call psychosis — where the mind loses touch with what’s real, with hearing voices and feeling watched. I know that word is scary, but I want you to hear this clearly: it is a recognised illness, it is treatable, and getting help early genuinely makes a difference."

"Let me ask some important things to keep him safe. Has he said or done anything to hurt himself, or talked about not wanting to be here? Is there any risk he might hurt someone, or do the voices tell him to do things? Is he eating and drinking? … And right now, behind that door, do you feel safe in the house?"

"Can I stop you on one thing — you asked if it’s your fault for not spotting the cannabis sooner. It is NOT your fault. Cannabis can play a part, yes, but this is an illness, not a parenting failure or a punishment. You noticing now and ringing is exactly what he needs."

"And I sense there might be a bigger fear — is there any history of something like this in the family? … His dad. I understand why you’re terrified he’ll be ‘locked away forever’. Let me be honest and hopeful: most young people with this are treated in the community, with support, and many recover well, especially when it’s caught early like this. This is not a life sentence."

"So here’s what happens now: I’m going to arrange an urgent mental-health assessment today — there are specialist teams for exactly this in young people, and they can often come to you rather than you having to get him out. I’ll speak to our duty doctor and the crisis team. He may not want to engage, and that’s okay — they’re used to that."

"While we set that up: keep things calm, don’t argue with the beliefs but don’t pretend to share them — just stay gentle and present. If at any point he tries to harm himself or anyone else, or you feel in danger, call 999 and say it’s a mental-health emergency. I’ll ring you back to confirm the assessment and I’ll make sure you’re supported too — you can’t pour from an empty cup. You are not on your own with this."

f.learning: Weeks of progressive withdrawal, insomnia, auditory hallucinations, persecutory and referential delusions (the TV "watching/sending messages"), functional decline and self-protective behaviour in a teenager is probable first-episode psychosis — a serious but treatable condition where early intervention improves outcomes, and must not be dismissed as "just drugs" or "a phase". The tasks: recognise it, assess risk through the collateral history (self-harm/suicide, harm to others, command hallucinations, ability to stay safe, household safety), and arrange URGENT same-day assessment via the Early Intervention in Psychosis/crisis pathway (NICE CG155: urgent referral for a first presentation of sustained psychotic symptoms; no antipsychotic started in primary care without a consultant child and adolescent psychiatrist), with home-based assessment for a young person who won’t engage and 999/police if there is immediate danger. Cannabis is a relevant precipitant but not a blame narrative. The examinable hidden agenda is the mother’s guilt ("I caused it by missing the cannabis") and her unspoken terror that he has inherited his father’s illness and will be "locked away forever" — address both with compassion and honest, hopeful information about community treatment and recovery, and support the family. A concrete, coordinated safety plan, not just information, wins the station.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG155 (psychosis and schizophrenia in children and young people, 2013, updated 2016) · NICE CG178 (2014) · NICE QS80 (2015) · Mental Health Act 1983 · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018)
knowledge.summary: Weeks of voices, feeling watched, messages from the TV, withdrawal and barricading in a 17-year-old is probable first-episode psychosis. Assess risk through his mother, and refer urgently to the early intervention in psychosis service or CAMHS, today if risk is raised.

points.h: Recognise it from the collateral history
points.t: Hallucinations, persecutory and referential delusions, social withdrawal, insomnia and a fall in function over weeks point to psychosis. A frightened young person who barricades himself is usually acting on fear. Ask about other drugs, head injury, fever or confusion, which suggest an organic or toxic cause.

NICE CG155: a first presentation of sustained psychotic symptoms (4 weeks or more) should be referred urgently to a specialist mental health service, either CAMHS or an early intervention in psychosis (EIP) service for those aged 14 and over. Where risk is raised, the crisis team or on-call CAMHS assesses the same day.

points.h: Do not start antipsychotics in primary care
points.t: NICE CG155: do not start antipsychotic medication for a first presentation of sustained psychotic symptoms in primary care unless it is done in consultation with a consultant psychiatrist with training in child and adolescent mental health.

points.h: Assess risk, do not score it
points.t: Through his mother: thoughts or acts of self-harm or suicide, threats or aggression, voices telling him to act, access to weapons or means, eating and drinking, and her own safety. NICE NG225 (2022) advises against using risk tools or low/medium/high labels to decide care; use the whole picture.

points.h: Cannabis: part of the story, not the verdict
points.t: Heavy and high-potency cannabis use is associated with a higher risk of psychosis. It does not change the need for urgent assessment, and the EIP team treats both. Blame closes doors for the young person and the family.

Crisis and EIP teams can assess at home. If there is immediate danger, call 999. If he refuses assessment and the risk is serious, a Mental Health Act 1983 assessment is arranged through an approved mental health professional (AMHP). At 16 or 17, a parent cannot consent to informal admission on behalf of a young person with capacity who refuses (Mental Health Act 1983, s131).

NHS England’s EIP access standard (NICE QS80) expects treatment to start within 2 weeks of referral. Most young people with a first episode are treated in the community, with family intervention and CBT alongside medication (NICE CG155), and many recover well.

dg.d: Checked immediate safety, then let the mother describe the weeks of change in her own words before narrowing.
College, sleep, cannabis, who is at home, the mother’s exhaustion and who can support her today.
Collateral mental state picture; asks about other drugs, head injury, fever or confusion; physical checks and bloods are left to the specialist assessment.
First-episode psychosis; substance-induced psychosis; mood disorder with psychotic features; organic or toxic cause.
Self-harm, suicide, command voices, aggression, eating and drinking, access to means, and the mother’s safety asked explicitly.
Names probable first-episode psychosis in plain words, as a treatable illness needing urgent assessment.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day crisis or EIP/CAMHS assessment at home; no antipsychotic started in primary care; calm, non-confrontational advice for home.
Cannabis handled as a contributor without blame; the mother’s wellbeing and support addressed.
999 for immediate danger, NHS 111 mental health option, timed call-back, documentation.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “is it my fault?” and the hesitation about the family, and explored both.
Idea (drugs or a breakdown); concern (guilt, his father’s illness, “locked away forever”); expectation (to know who to call).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — guilt that she "caused it" by missing the cannabis, and unspoken terror that he has inherited his father’s "breakdown" (possible family psychosis) and will be "locked away forever" — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery, returning your call about Daniel. Before anything else, are you somewhere you can talk, and is everyone in the house safe right now?
model.why: Checks immediate safety before gathering the story

model.text: (Lowered voice.) Yes, I’m downstairs. He’s in his room. He’s pushed the wardrobe against the door. Doctor, he’s saying people are watching him through the telly. Is he on drugs? Is he having a breakdown? I don’t know who to call.

You’ve done exactly the right thing by ringing. I can hear how frightened you are. I’d like to understand what’s been happening, check he and you are safe, and then agree what happens today. Is that all right?
model.why: Acknowledges fear and sets a clear agenda

model.text: Yes. Please.
Tell me about the change in him, from when you first noticed something was different.
model.why: Open question lets her tell the story in her own order

model.text: A few weeks ago he stopped going to college. He’s up all night. He hardly comes out. Then he started saying he could hear people talking about him, and that the TV is sending him messages. Today he barricaded the door.
Has he said what the voices say? Do they ever tell him to do things, like hurt himself or someone else?
He says they talk about him, say he’s being watched. He’s never said they tell him to do anything.
Has he said or done anything to suggest he wants to harm himself, or talked about not wanting to be here? And has he been aggressive or threatening to anyone?
model.why: Explicit risk to self and others through the collateral history

model.text: No. He’s not violent. He just seems terrified.
Is he eating and drinking? And is there anything in his room he could hurt himself with, or any tablets he could get to?
I think he’s eating something. I don’t think there’s anything in there… I’m not sure.
Has he been using any drugs or alcohol that you know of, and has he had a head injury, a fever or seemed confused?
model.why: Screens for substances and organic causes

model.text: Cannabis. A lot, this last year. No injury, no fever. (Pause.) Is it the drugs? Is it my fault? I should have stopped it sooner.

Can I stop on that, because it matters. This is not your fault. Cannabis can play a part in this, yes, but what Daniel is going through is an illness, not a failure of parenting. You noticing and ringing is exactly what he needs.
model.why: Responds directly to the guilt cue

model.text: (Crying.) I just keep thinking I missed it.
You’re carrying a lot. I wonder if there’s a bigger fear underneath. Is there anything in the family that this reminds you of?
model.why: Opens the door to the unspoken family-history fear

model.text: His dad had a breakdown. I’m scared Daniel’s got the same thing, and they’ll lock him away forever.

Thank you for telling me. That fear makes complete sense. Let me be honest and hopeful: most young people with this are treated at home, with a specialist team, and many recover well, especially when help starts early, as it is today. Being locked away forever is not what happens.
model.why: Addresses the hidden agenda with honest, hopeful information

model.text: From what you describe, Daniel may be having what we call psychosis. It means the mind is struggling to tell what’s real, so voices and feeling watched seem completely true to him. It’s a recognised illness, it’s treatable, and the sooner specialists see him, the better it tends to go.
model.why: Names probable first-episode psychosis in plain language

model.text: So it’s not just the drugs?
The cannabis may have been a trigger, and the team will help him with it. But either way, this needs the same urgent assessment. It isn’t something to wait and see about.
model.why: Places cannabis correctly without making it the whole story

model.text: Here’s the plan. As soon as we finish, I’ll contact the crisis team and the early intervention team, who specialise in young people with this, and ask for an assessment today. They can come to the house, so you won’t have to get him out.
model.why: Urgent same-day referral via the right pathway, with home assessment

model.text: What if he won’t open the door?

They’re used to that. Until they arrive, keep things calm. Don’t argue with what he believes, but don’t pretend to agree either. Tell him you’re worried, you love him and help is coming. Don’t try to force the door.
model.why: Practical de-escalation advice for the parent

model.text: And you matter in this too. Is there someone who can be with you today? Once things are settled, the team can support you as a family, and there are carers’ groups for parents going through exactly this.
model.why: Supports the exhausted parent as well as the patient

model.text: I can ring someone to come over.

Good. If at any point he tries to hurt himself or anyone, or you feel unsafe, ring 999 and say it’s a mental health emergency. If you’re worried but it’s not an emergency, call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. I’ll ring you back within the hour to confirm the assessment time.
model.why: Clear escalation routes and a timed call-back

model.text: Thank you. I didn’t know any of this existed.
So we’re clear, can you tell me what you’ll do if things get worse before the team arrives?
Call 999 if he tries to hurt himself or me. Otherwise wait for you to ring back, and keep calm with him.
Exactly right. I’ll document everything, and we won’t leave you on your own with this. Is there anything else you want to ask before I make those calls?
model.why: Summarises, shares the floor and commits to continuity

model.text: No. Just please ring me back.

social.t: A frightened, exhausted parent managing a young person who won’t engage. Ask who can be with her and signpost carer support (for example Rethink Mental Illness or the YoungMinds parents helpline).
He has stopped college. Once he is under the EIP team, education and occupational support is part of recovery; the college can be involved with his consent.

legal.t: At 16 and 17 a young person is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005) and can consent to treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8). A parent cannot consent to informal admission for a 16- or 17-year-old with capacity who refuses (Mental Health Act 1983, s131).
If he refuses assessment and there is serious risk, an AMHP coordinates a Mental Health Act 1983 assessment. Police cannot use s136 inside a private home; entry to a home needs a s135 warrant.
If he holds a licence, including a provisional one, an acute psychotic episode must be notified to the DVLA and he should not drive (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: GMC 0–18 years: listening to a parent’s concerns and giving general information does not breach his confidentiality. Share his information with her proportionately, in his best interests and with his agreement where possible.
Record the collateral history, the risk questions and answers, who was contacted and when, and the call-back. Name a clinician for follow-up.

community.t: NHS 111 mental health option (24/7) for urgent advice; 999 when there is immediate danger. Local crisis and EIP teams can assess at home.

playbook.diagnosisLay: “Psychosis is when the mind struggles to tell what’s real and what isn’t. To Daniel, the voices and being watched feel completely real, which is why he’s so frightened. With the right help, most young people get much better.”

management.psychosocial: Support the mother: someone with her today, carer support, and a named person at the practice. Advise calm, gentle contact without arguing with his beliefs.
sharedPlan: Urgent same-day assessment via the crisis team and EIP/CAMHS, at home if needed
No antipsychotic started in primary care; specialist team leads treatment
Cannabis addressed by the specialist team as part of care, not as blame
safetyNet: 999 and “mental health emergency” if he tries to harm himself or others or she feels unsafe

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station is failed by treating a first episode of psychosis as a drug problem or a routine referral, and by missing the mother’s guilt and fear. The patterns below come up again and again in examiner feedback.

items.fail: “It’s probably the cannabis. Get him to stop and bring him in if he’s no better.”
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK practice.” NICE CG155 calls for urgent specialist referral for sustained psychotic symptoms.
items.fix: Name probable psychosis and arrange same-day crisis or EIP assessment, whatever the role of cannabis.

items.fail: No risk questions because the mother says he isn’t violent.
items.why: “Does not assess risk adequately.” Command voices, suicidal thoughts, means and self-care must be asked about directly.
items.fix: Ask about voices telling him to act, self-harm, aggression, eating and drinking, means, and her own safety.

items.fail: Booking him into surgery next week, or suggesting she brings him in.
items.why: A barricaded young person won’t attend. A plan that can’t happen scores nothing.
items.fix: “The team can come to him today.” Explain what to do if he won’t open the door.

items.fail: Hearing “is it my fault?” and moving straight on to questions.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” Her guilt shapes everything she hears next.
items.fix: Stop and answer it: “It is not your fault.” Then ask gently about the family.

items.fail: Never finding out about his father, so the “locked away forever” fear is left unanswered.
items.why: The hidden agenda carries the Relating marks in this station.
items.fix: “Is there anything in the family this reminds you of?” Then give honest, hopeful information about community treatment.

items.fail: Reading out a list of phone numbers and ending the call.
items.why: “Safety-netting not specific” and “no follow-up arranged” are common failing statements.
items.fix: Specific triggers for 999, the NHS 111 mental health option, a timed call-back, and teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Treats it as “just cannabis” or a teenage phase; offers a routine appointment for when he’ll come in; no risk questions; blames or lectures the mother; leaves her with a list of numbers and no plan.
wordPics.pass: Recognises probable psychosis; asks about self-harm, aggression and command voices; arranges urgent specialist assessment; gives 999 advice; reassures that it is not her fault.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: checks immediate safety at the start; surfaces the father’s illness and the “locked away forever” fear and answers it with honest hope; arranges a home assessment today and a timed call-back; gives practical advice on staying calm with him; makes sure she has support; checks understanding.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like the cannabis. If he stops smoking it he’ll probably settle down.”
avoid.instead: “Cannabis may have played a part, but this needs a specialist to see him today, whatever the cause.”
avoid.why: Reducing it to drugs delays urgent assessment and blames the young person.

avoid.dont: “Can you bring him in to see me next week?”
avoid.instead: “He doesn’t need to come to us. I’ll ask the crisis team to come to him today.”
avoid.why: A barricaded young person with psychosis won’t attend; the plan has to fit the reality.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, lots of teenagers go through phases.”

avoid.why: False reassurance ignores serious symptoms and her real fear.

SCA_MODELS.text: Cannabis. A lot, this last year. No injury, no fever. (Pause.) Is it the drugs? Is it my fault? I should have stopped it sooner.

Can I stop on that, because it matters. This is not your fault. Cannabis can play a part in this, yes, but what Daniel is going through is an illness, not a failure of parenting. You noticing and ringing is exactly what he needs.
SCA_MODELS.why: Responds directly to the guilt cue

SCA_MODELS.text: (Crying.) I just keep thinking I missed it.
You’re carrying a lot. I wonder if there’s a bigger fear underneath. Is there anything in the family that this reminds you of?
SCA_MODELS.why: Opens the door to the unspoken family-history fear

SCA_MODELS.text: His dad had a breakdown. I’m scared Daniel’s got the same thing, and they’ll lock him away forever.

Thank you for telling me. That fear makes complete sense. Let me be honest and hopeful: most young people with this are treated at home, with a specialist team, and many recover well, especially when help starts early, as it is today. Being locked away forever is not what happens.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the hidden agenda with honest, hopeful information

SCA_MODELS.text: From what you describe, Daniel may be having what we call psychosis. It means the mind is struggling to tell what’s real, so voices and feeling watched seem completely true to him. It’s a recognised illness, it’s treatable, and the sooner specialists see him, the better it tends to go.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names probable first-episode psychosis in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s not just the drugs?
The cannabis may have been a trigger, and the team will help him with it. But either way, this needs the same urgent assessment. It isn’t something to wait and see about.
SCA_MODELS.why: Places cannabis correctly without making it the whole story

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s the plan. As soon as we finish, I’ll contact the crisis team and the early intervention team, who specialise in young people with this, and ask for an assessment today. They can come to the house, so you won’t have to get him out.
SCA_MODELS.why: Urgent same-day referral via the right pathway, with home assessment

SCA_MODELS.text: What if he won’t open the door?

They’re used to that. Until they arrive, keep things calm. Don’t argue with what he believes, but don’t pretend to agree either. Tell him you’re worried, you love him and help is coming. Don’t try to force the door.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical de-escalation advice for the parent

SCA_MODELS.text: And you matter in this too. Is there someone who can be with you today? Once things are settled, the team can support you as a family, and there are carers’ groups for parents going through exactly this.
SCA_MODELS.why: Supports the exhausted parent as well as the patient

SCA_MODELS.text: I can ring someone to come over.

Good. If at any point he tries to hurt himself or anyone, or you feel unsafe, ring 999 and say it’s a mental health emergency. If you’re worried but it’s not an emergency, call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. I’ll ring you back within the hour to confirm the assessment time.
SCA_MODELS.why: Clear escalation routes and a timed call-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. I didn’t know any of this existed.
So we’re clear, can you tell me what you’ll do if things get worse before the team arrives?
Call 999 if he tries to hurt himself or me. Otherwise wait for you to ring back, and keep calm with him.
Exactly right. I’ll document everything, and we won’t leave you on your own with this. Is there anything else you want to ask before I make those calls?
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises, shares the floor and commits to continuity

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Just please ring me back.

SCA_STEM.name: Daniel
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations recorded. Lives at home with his mother. Was attending college.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call from his mother, who is worried about a sudden change in his behaviour over recent weeks. Daniel is at home but will not come to the phone.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG155 (psychosis and schizophrenia in children and young people, 2013, updated 2016) · NICE CG178 (2014) · NICE QS80 (2015) · Mental Health Act 1983 · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Weeks of voices, feeling watched, messages from the TV, withdrawal and barricading in a 17-year-old is probable first-episode psychosis. Assess risk through his mother, and refer urgently to the early intervention in psychosis service or CAMHS, today if risk is raised.

points.h: Recognise it from the collateral history
points.t: Hallucinations, persecutory and referential delusions, social withdrawal, insomnia and a fall in function over weeks point to psychosis. A frightened young person who barricades himself is usually acting on fear. Ask about other drugs, head injury, fever or confusion, which suggest an organic or toxic cause.

NICE CG155: a first presentation of sustained psychotic symptoms (4 weeks or more) should be referred urgently to a specialist mental health service, either CAMHS or an early intervention in psychosis (EIP) service for those aged 14 and over. Where risk is raised, the crisis team or on-call CAMHS assesses the same day.

points.h: Do not start antipsychotics in primary care
points.t: NICE CG155: do not start antipsychotic medication for a first presentation of sustained psychotic symptoms in primary care unless it is done in consultation with a consultant psychiatrist with training in child and adolescent mental health.

points.h: Assess risk, do not score it
points.t: Through his mother: thoughts or acts of self-harm or suicide, threats or aggression, voices telling him to act, access to weapons or means, eating and drinking, and her own safety. NICE NG225 (2022) advises against using risk tools or low/medium/high labels to decide care; use the whole picture.

points.h: Cannabis: part of the story, not the verdict
points.t: Heavy and high-potency cannabis use is associated with a higher risk of psychosis. It does not change the need for urgent assessment, and the EIP team treats both. Blame closes doors for the young person and the family.

Crisis and EIP teams can assess at home. If there is immediate danger, call 999. If he refuses assessment and the risk is serious, a Mental Health Act 1983 assessment is arranged through an approved mental health professional (AMHP). At 16 or 17, a parent cannot consent to informal admission on behalf of a young person with capacity who refuses (Mental Health Act 1983, s131).

NHS England’s EIP access standard (NICE QS80) expects treatment to start within 2 weeks of referral. Most young people with a first episode are treated in the community, with family intervention and CBT alongside medication (NICE CG155), and many recover well.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked immediate safety, then let the mother describe the weeks of change in her own words before narrowing.
College, sleep, cannabis, who is at home, the mother’s exhaustion and who can support her today.
Picked up “is it my fault?” and the hesitation about the family, and explored both.
Idea (drugs or a breakdown); concern (guilt, his father’s illness, “locked away forever”); expectation (to know who to call).
Collateral mental state picture; asks about other drugs, head injury, fever or confusion; physical checks and bloods are left to the specialist assessment.
First-episode psychosis; substance-induced psychosis; mood disorder with psychotic features; organic or toxic cause.
Self-harm, suicide, command voices, aggression, eating and drinking, access to means, and the mother’s safety asked explicitly.
Names probable first-episode psychosis in plain words, as a treatable illness needing urgent assessment.
Same-day crisis or EIP/CAMHS assessment at home; no antipsychotic started in primary care; calm, non-confrontational advice for home.
Cannabis handled as a contributor without blame; the mother’s wellbeing and support addressed.
999 for immediate danger, NHS 111 mental health option, timed call-back, documentation.

social.t: A frightened, exhausted parent managing a young person who won’t engage. Ask who can be with her and signpost carer support (for example Rethink Mental Illness or the YoungMinds parents helpline).
He has stopped college. Once he is under the EIP team, education and occupational support is part of recovery; the college can be involved with his consent.

legal.t: At 16 and 17 a young person is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005) and can consent to treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969, s8). A parent cannot consent to informal admission for a 16- or 17-year-old with capacity who refuses (Mental Health Act 1983, s131).
If he refuses assessment and there is serious risk, an AMHP coordinates a Mental Health Act 1983 assessment. Police cannot use s136 inside a private home; entry to a home needs a s135 warrant.
If he holds a licence, including a provisional one, an acute psychotic episode must be notified to the DVLA and he should not drive (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: GMC 0–18 years: listening to a parent’s concerns and giving general information does not breach his confidentiality. Share his information with her proportionately, in his best interests and with his agreement where possible.
Record the collateral history, the risk questions and answers, who was contacted and when, and the call-back. Name a clinician for follow-up.

community.t: NHS 111 mental health option (24/7) for urgent advice; 999 when there is immediate danger. Local crisis and EIP teams can assess at home.

redFlags: Voices telling him to harm himself or others, or plans to act on persecutory beliefs
Talk of suicide, self-harm, or access to weapons, tablets or other means
Not eating or drinking, confusion, fever or head injury (consider an organic cause)
psychosocial: College dropped, social withdrawal, heavy cannabis use over the last year
Mother frightened and exhausted: who can support her today?
Family history (his father’s “breakdown”) as a sensitive factor, raised gently
ice: Idea: “Is he on drugs, or having a breakdown?”
Concern: guilt that she missed the cannabis; fear he has his father’s illness and will be “locked away forever”
Expectation: to be told what it is and who to call

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “From what you’re telling me, Daniel may be having a first episode of psychosis. It’s a recognised and treatable illness, and it needs a specialist assessment today rather than waiting.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Psychosis is when the mind struggles to tell what’s real and what isn’t. To Daniel, the voices and being watched feel completely real, which is why he’s so frightened. With the right help, most young people get much better.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if this is your fault. It isn’t. And I know you’re scared it’s what happened to his dad, and that he’ll be locked away. Most young people are treated at home, and many recover well.”
management.psychosocial: Support the mother: someone with her today, carer support, and a named person at the practice. Advise calm, gentle contact without arguing with his beliefs.
sharedPlan: Urgent same-day assessment via the crisis team and EIP/CAMHS, at home if needed
No antipsychotic started in primary care; specialist team leads treatment
Cannabis addressed by the specialist team as part of care, not as blame
safetyNet: 999 and “mental health emergency” if he tries to harm himself or others or she feels unsafe
NHS 111 mental health option for urgent advice; GP call-back at an agreed time

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station is failed by treating a first episode of psychosis as a drug problem or a routine referral, and by missing the mother’s guilt and fear. The patterns below come up again and again in examiner feedback.

items.fail: “It’s probably the cannabis. Get him to stop and bring him in if he’s no better.”
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK practice.” NICE CG155 calls for urgent specialist referral for sustained psychotic symptoms.
items.fix: Name probable psychosis and arrange same-day crisis or EIP assessment, whatever the role of cannabis.

items.fail: No risk questions because the mother says he isn’t violent.
items.why: “Does not assess risk adequately.” Command voices, suicidal thoughts, means and self-care must be asked about directly.
items.fix: Ask about voices telling him to act, self-harm, aggression, eating and drinking, means, and her own safety.

items.fail: Booking him into surgery next week, or suggesting she brings him in.
items.why: A barricaded young person won’t attend. A plan that can’t happen scores nothing.
items.fix: “The team can come to him today.” Explain what to do if he won’t open the door.

items.fail: Hearing “is it my fault?” and moving straight on to questions.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” Her guilt shapes everything she hears next.
items.fix: Stop and answer it: “It is not your fault.” Then ask gently about the family.

items.fail: Never finding out about his father, so the “locked away forever” fear is left unanswered.
items.why: The hidden agenda carries the Relating marks in this station.
items.fix: “Is there anything in the family this reminds you of?” Then give honest, hopeful information about community treatment.

items.fail: Reading out a list of phone numbers and ending the call.
items.why: “Safety-netting not specific” and “no follow-up arranged” are common failing statements.
items.fix: Specific triggers for 999, the NHS 111 mental health option, a timed call-back, and teach-back.
